reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / American Academy of Ophthalmology BCSC (External Disease and Cornea)
clinicalPearls: A bilateral, slowly progressive corneal endothelial dystrophy, more common in women and typically becoming symptomatic in later middle age and beyond
The earliest sign is corneal guttata: focal excrescences of Descemet membrane seen as an irregular beaten-metal appearance on the endothelium
As endothelial cell loss progresses, the cornea can no longer be kept dehydrated, leading to stromal and epithelial oedema
Patients classically report vision that is worst on waking and improves through the day, because lid closure overnight reduces evaporative dehydration
Advanced disease causes painful epithelial bullae (bullous keratopathy) that can rupture and cause recurrent erosions
Specular and confocal microscopy quantify endothelial cell density and morphology, and pachymetry tracks corneal thickness as a marker of decompensation
There is a recognised genetic basis, including associations with certain gene variants, and cataract surgery can accelerate decompensation in a marginal cornea
Management principles range from hypertonic saline and lowering intraocular pressure early, to endothelial keratoplasty for visually significant oedema
reference.pathophysiology: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy is a degenerative disorder of the corneal endothelium, the monolayer of non-dividing cells that pumps fluid out of the stroma to keep the cornea clear. Accelerated endothelial cell loss and the deposition of abnormal extracellular matrix produce guttata (focal thickenings of Descemet membrane). As endothelial cell density falls below the level needed to maintain deturgescence, fluid accumulates in the stroma and epithelium, causing corneal oedema, loss of transparency and eventually painful bullae. Oxidative stress, genetic predisposition and endothelial dysfunction all contribute, and any additional insult such as intraocular surgery can tip a borderline cornea into frank decompensation.
additionalDifferentials: Corneal oedema from chronically raised intraocular pressure
Toxic anterior segment or post-surgical endothelial decompensation
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to identify guttata, stromal and epithelial oedema and bullae
Specular microscopy to measure endothelial cell density and morphology
Confocal microscopy for detailed endothelial assessment when the cornea is oedematous
Corneal pachymetry to quantify thickness and monitor for progressive oedema
Corneal tomography to assess overall corneal structure before surgery
Assessment of cataract and surgical risk to plan combined or staged intervention
redFlags: Painful bullous keratopathy with recurrent epithelial breakdown
Rapid corneal decompensation, particularly after intraocular surgery
Marked reduction in endothelial cell density threatening imminent decompensation before planned surgery
Corneal infection or ulceration complicating ruptured bullae
reference.prognosis: Progression is typically slow over years; many patients remain functionally comfortable with conservative measures, and endothelial keratoplasty offers good visual rehabilitation for advanced disease, though transplantation carries risks of rejection and may need to be repeated.
pitfalls: Failing to assess endothelial reserve before cataract surgery and precipitating decompensation
Attributing morning visual blur to other causes and missing early endothelial disease
Mistaking guttata alone for visually significant dystrophy when vision loss has another cause
Overlooking coexisting glaucoma that worsens corneal oedema
Delaying keratoplasty until painful bullae and scarring compromise the surgical outcome
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course
management: Topical hypertonic sodium chloride drops and ointment to reduce stromal and epithelial oedema and improve early-day vision
Reduce the evaporative load on waking with warm-air drying to ease morning blurring
Bandage contact lens and ocular lubricants for symptomatic bullous keratopathy
Definitive endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK or DSAEK) for decompensated corneas, reserving penetrating keratoplasty for advanced scarred disease
Careful cataract assessment with endothelial-sparing surgery, and combined or staged keratoplasty when decompensation is likely
Serial specular microscopy and pachymetry to track endothelial loss and time surgery
Post-transplant topical corticosteroids with monitoring for graft rejection and failure
